title: Three Words, Two Strikes
subtitle: The Smoke and Fire of the Market — What Soothes the Common Heart
description: "Three Words, Two Strikes" is the collective name for Feng Menglong's compiled Stories to Enlighten the World, Stories to Warn the World, and Stories to Awaken the World, together with Ling Mengchu's Slapping the Table in Amazement (First Collection) and Slapping the Table in Amazement (Second Collection). Together they comprise nearly two hundred short vernacular stories, forming the great synthesis of classical Chinese vernacular short fiction. Drawn from market life, commercial legends, and romantic joys and sorrows, these stories vividly depict the full range of human experience and the flourishing urban landscapes of Ming-dynasty Jiangnan towns.

route.title: Three Words, Two Strikes: The Prosperous Jiangnan — A Picture of Human Life
route.intro:
To understand the ways of the world is knowledge; to be versed in human affairs is literature.
Feng Menglong (1574–1646), style name Youlong, literary name Master of Mohanzhai, was a native of Changzhou County, Suzhou Prefecture. Ling Mengchu (1580–1644), style name Xuanfang, literary name Chucheng, was from Wucheng, Zhejiang. Both were talented scholars of late-Ming Jiangnan, living in the Suzhou-Hangzhou region where the printing industry flourished and urban culture thrived. Their writing penetrated deep into the life of the market — the oil seller who won the flower queen, Du Shiniang who angrily sank her jewel chest, Lady White Snake forever imprisoned beneath Leifeng Pagoda. These stories contain no grand narratives of emperors and generals, only the joys and sorrows of ordinary people — and precisely for that reason, they are all the more true and moving. Let us enter the Jiangnan world of Three Words, Two Strikes — from Suzhou gardens to Hangzhou's West Lake, from Nanjing's Qinhuai River to Huizhou's ancient villages — visiting the national heritage sites that bear witness to the bustle of the market and the true feelings of the human heart.

stops.title: Stop One: Suzhou · The Jiangnan Dream Deep Within the Gardens
stops.content: Most stories in Three Words, Two Strikes take place in the towns of Jiangnan, and Suzhou is the most important setting of all — it was on the streets of Suzhou that the oil seller Qin Zhong was hawking his wares when he met the flower queen. Mid-to-late Ming Suzhou was the most prosperous commercial city in the nation, leading the world in silk weaving and printing. The saying "When Suzhou and Huzhou are well-harvested, the empire has enough to eat" was known across the land. The Humble Administrator's Garden is the ultimate Suzhou classical garden — water is the main element, with pavilions, terraces, and towers built along the water's edge, "though made by man, as if opened by heaven." The Lingering Garden is famed for its layered architectural spaces and masterful rock and water techniques. Walking through the garden's covered corridors, the Taihu limestone rocks are exquisitely translucent, the gentle ripples of blue water reflecting the white walls and black tiles — the love and heartache that unfolded in the deep courtyards of Three Words, Two Strikes seem hidden behind every lattice window. The Humble Administrator's Garden was first built in the fourth year of Zhengde, Ming (1509 AD) by Imperial Censor Wang Xianchen, taking sixteen years to complete. It covers seventy-eight mu, making it the largest surviving classical garden in Suzhou. The garden is divided into eastern, central, and western sections, with the central section being the finest — the Fragrant Snow Pavilion sits by the lotus pond; when the lotuses bloom in summer, a gentle breeze brings their fragrance through the hall. Sitting on the beauty-rest railing of the Fragrant Snow Pavilion, before you lies the shimmering lotus pond with the Snow-Fragrance Cloud-Viewing Pavilion on the rockery, and at your ears the rustle of wind through the bamboo grove. The stories Feng Menglong wrote — tales unfolding in the secluded boudoirs and embroidered chambers — "Jiang Xingge Reunites with the Pearl Shirt," "Jin Yunu Beats the Ungrateful Lover" — take place in just such exquisite, deep courtyard settings. Every lattice window is a picture frame: framing the banana palm, framing the lake stone, framing the distant hills — and framing the youth and sorrow of the women of that era. A short walk from the Humble Administrator's Garden brings you to the Lingering Garden. The Lingering Garden's Cloud-Capped Peak stone stands 6.5 meters tall, the largest Taihu limestone south of the Yangtze — combining the four beauties of leanness, transparency, perforation, and wrinkle, like a miniature immortal mountain. The Lingering Garden's spatial sequence is another marvel: from the narrow entrance corridor to the sudden spaciousness of the main hall, then to the layered progression of the courtyards — "scenery changes with every step," "views beyond views." Is this not also the art of Feng Menglong and Ling Mengchu's fiction? A seemingly ordinary opening, then a door opens into another world; a seemingly mundane account of market affairs, and around the corner lies the abyss of human nature. In "The Oil Seller Wins the Flower Queen," Qin Zhong is merely a peddler carrying his oil load through the streets, yet he wins the heart of the flower queen Xin Yaoqin with his pure sincerity — the story's turning point is like one of those unexpected doorways in the Lingering Garden: you only see the most beautiful scene after you pass through. The beauty of Suzhou gardens lies not in their size but in the surprise hidden at every turn — just like Three Words, Two Strikes, where the truest feelings of the Chinese heart lie hidden amid the smoke and fire of the market.

stops.title: Stop Two: Hangzhou · The Mortal Romance Amid West Lake's Mist and Rain
stops.content: "Lady White Snake Forever Imprisoned Beneath Leifeng Pagoda" — the earliest version of the White Snake legend first appears in Stories to Warn the World. Xu Xian and Bai Suzhen meet on the Broken Bridge at West Lake, borrowing an umbrella as a token of their love — the most beloved love story in China took root in the landscape of Hangzhou. And in Three Words, Two Strikes, countless small vendors, artisans, and down-and-out scholars also play out their own joys and sorrows in this prosperous old capital of the Southern Song. The Feilai Peak Sculptures (including the West Lake South Mountain Sculptures) feature over three hundred Buddhist statues from the Five Dynasties to the Yuan dynasty, with the kind-eyed, broad-bellied Maitreya smiling at the world from the cliff face for a thousand years. And the Lingyin Temple Stone Pagodas and Sutra Pillars — two Song-dynasty stone pagodas and two Five Dynasties sutra pillars stand quietly before the temple, having witnessed the stories of countless devotees. The waters of West Lake are still as gentle, and the chance encounters and romances of Three Words, Two Strikes seem to play out again on the Broken Bridge every rainy day. Chapter Twenty-Eight of Stories to Warn the World, "Lady White Snake Forever Imprisoned Beneath Leifeng Pagoda," is one of the most celebrated tales in all of Three Words, Two Strikes. The story's Xu Xuan is a young Hangzhou man working as a pharmacy assistant. During the Qingming Festival, he encounters rain while visiting West Lake and meets Lady White Snake and her maid Xiaoqing on the Broken Bridge. Using the borrowed umbrella as a pretext to arrange a meeting the next day for its return — the curtain rises on the most romantic love legend in China, gently drawn open amid the mist and rain of West Lake. Standing on the Broken Bridge, the West Lake in April is veiled in misty drizzle, the distant hills like dark eyebrows, the nearby water wrapped in haze — the slender silhouette of Baochu Pagoda appears and disappears in the rain and fog. It is precisely this kind of scenery that gave birth to such moving imagination: a thousand-year serpent taking human form, just to experience human love once. The Feilai Peak Sculptures (including the West Lake South Mountain Sculptures) are distributed across the cliffs of Feilai Peak before Lingyin Temple, with over three hundred cave and cliff sculptures. The most famous is the Song-dynasty Maitreya Buddha — big-bellied, wide-mouthed in laughter, one hand fingering prayer beads, the other resting on his knee. This Maitreya is carved into the cliff face beside the path, about two meters tall, and thousands of tourists pass before him every day — he gazes at them all with a smile, as if saying: "I understand all these human loves and sorrows." Maitreya's compassion and Leifeng Pagoda's cruelty form a curious balance in the ripples of West Lake — it was not the Buddha's law that constrained Lady White Snake, but the rules of the human world; and what fulfilled Xu Xuan was not the Buddha's law either, but his half-real, half-illusory attachment to Lady White Snake. Lady White Snake was ultimately imprisoned beneath Leifeng Pagoda, but her story flew out from beneath the pagoda — flew over mountains, flew over seas, and flew into the heart of every Chinese person.

stops.title: Stop Three: Nanjing · The Warmth and Coldness of the World Amid Qinhuai Romance
stops.content: Nanjing was the Ming auxiliary capital and a city that appears frequently in Three Words, Two Strikes. The story of "Du Shiniang Angrily Sinks the Jewel Chest" is set in Nanjing — Li Jia meets Du Shiniang in the pleasure quarters along the Qinhuai River, only to sell her to a salt merchant at the Yangtze ferry on his way home. Du Shiniang, one by one, displays her jewels on the boat's prow, then sinks them all into the river, and throws herself in after them — sacrificing herself for her love and her dignity. The spirit-way of the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum winds through the forests and hills, setting the precedent for over five hundred years of Ming and Qing imperial tombs. And the Zhan Garden on the banks of the Qinhuai River was once the mansion of Xu Da, Prince Zhongshan of the Ming dynasty — the garden is deep, the rockeries jagged, the oar-sounds and lantern-reflections of the Qinhuai River faintly audible through the lattice windows. Three Words, Two Strikes was born in precisely this atmosphere: on one side, the solemn dignity of emperors and generals; on the other, the vivid life of the common market folk. The two interweave to form the truest portrait of late-Ming society. What makes Du Shiniang's story so heartbreaking is that her tragedy was not caused by a natural disaster or Heaven-sent calamity, but by the coldness of the human heart. Li Jia was not an evil man — he was merely a weak-willed son of a wealthy family who, faced with family pressure and worldly judgment, treated Du Shiniang as a commodity to be transferred. Chapter Thirty-Two of Stories to Warn the World writes: Du Shiniang opens her gold-lacquered dressing case on the boat, flinging luminous pearls, emeralds, and cat's-eyes one by one into the river, then hugs the jewel chest and leaps in — "her three souls vanished into the water palace, her seven spirits drifted into the dark road." The passage is written with restraint and cruelty — no hysterical accusations, only the ripples of jewels entering the water and the whispers from the surrounding merchant boats. The Zhan Garden by the Qinhuai River shares the same time and space as Du Shiniang's story. This princely garden, first built in the Ming Jiajing reign, takes rockeries as its main scene — the southern rockery rises in towering peaks with majestic force, the northern rockery winds in deep twists like a labyrinth. Within the garden is the Jingmiao Hall, three bays wide and built by the water. Sitting in the hall and gazing at the reflections in the pond, you can almost hear the pipa and the splash of oars on the Qinhuai River. The Ming dynasty's two-capital system allowed Nanjing to retain a full set of central government organs — the Six Ministries, the Imperial Academy, and the Censorate were all established here. Politically, Nanjing was the "leisure capital," but culturally, it was the "bustling capital." Large numbers of literati, retired officials, and wealthy merchants gathered here, giving rise to the unique "courtesan culture" along the Qinhuai River — and Du Shiniang's story is the most desolate footnote to that culture. From the solemn grandeur of the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum to the feasting and revelry of the Qinhuai River, from imperial achievement to a courtesan's leap into the river — the power of Three Words, Two Strikes lies in its ability to illuminate the joys and sorrows of every social class with an equal and compassionate gaze.

stops.title: Stop Four: Yangzhou · Ten Miles of Spring Breeze on the Yangzhou Road
stops.content: The stories of merchants in Three Words, Two Strikes are countless — and the Yangzhou salt merchants are among the most vividly portrayed. In the Ming dynasty, Yangzhou was the center of the Lianghuai salt transport, where wealthy merchants and magnates gathered, and ten-mile-long streets were packed with market stalls. The legends of overnight fortunes, the joys and sorrows of commercial success and failure, the romances between merchants' daughters and poor scholars — all unfold in the misty rain of Yangzhou. The Four-Season Rockeries at the Garden of Individuality are the pinnacle of Yangzhou garden rock-stacking art — the spring hills seem to smile, the summer hills seem to drip, the autumn hills seem to wear makeup, the winter hills seem to slumber. And the Lotus Bridge and White Pagoda on Slender West Lake stand gracefully above the blue waves. From Five-Pavilion Bridge, feeling the same Yangzhou wind that has blown for a thousand years, you understand why so many merchants in Three Words, Two Strikes could spend a lifetime wandering far away, yet the place they most wanted to return to was always Yangzhou — "ten miles of spring breeze." The Garden of Individuality was the private garden of Huang Zhiyun, the general manager of the Lianghuai salt industry in the Qing Jiaqing reign. The owner loved bamboo — the garden was planted with slender bamboos whose leaves resemble the character "个" (individual) — hence the name "Garden of Individuality." But what truly made this garden immortal is its uniquely conceived Four-Season Rockeries: bamboo-shoot stone with bamboo for spring, lake stone by the pond for summer, yellow stone building peaks for autumn, and white xuan stone spread like snow for winter. Standing before the winter rockery, the white xuan stone gleams coldly in the sunlight, with quartz fragments like remnants of snow scattered in the crevices — and from the latticed window of the winter garden, you can just glimpse the green bamboo of the spring garden, hinting that winter ends and spring returns, the endless cycle of life. Merchants valued profit, but Yangzhou salt merchants valued "taste" even more — they layered all their love of nature and their understanding of life into these stones. The Lotus Bridge and White Pagoda are the icons of Slender West Lake. The Lotus Bridge (Five-Pavilion Bridge) was built in the twenty-second year of Qing Qianlong (1757 AD). Five pavilions sit atop the bridge, with yellow tiles and vermilion columns, carved railings and painted beams. On full-moon nights, each of the fifteen bridge arches holds a moon, the moon in the sky and the moons in the water reflecting each other. The White Pagoda beside it was modeled after the White Dagoba in Beihai, Beijing. The legend that the pagoda was built overnight by piling up earth is still widely told. A famous tale in Three Words, Two Strikes is "The Lucky Merchant Encounters Dongting Red," about a down-on-his-luck merchant who suddenly turns his fortune around and becomes rich overnight — the White Pagoda's "overnight completion" legend and the lucky merchant's "overnight wealth" are both symbols of "luck" and "opportunity" in Jiangnan commercial culture. The most beautiful time in Yangzhou is the third month of spring — the qionghua flowers like snow, the willows like mist, the sound of strings and woodwinds drifting from boats on Slender West Lake. Sitting on the Five-Pavilion Bridge, feeling the March wind, you suddenly understand why the authors of Three Words, Two Strikes were so devoted to this city — because Yangzhou itself is a living Three Words, Two Strikes: every garden is a story, every lane hides a transaction, and every silhouette could be a legend.

stops.title: Stop Five: Huizhou · In a Former Life, Not Cultivated — Born in Huizhou
stops.content: The stories of Huizhou merchants in Three Words, Two Strikes are deeply moving. "In a former life, not cultivated — born in Huizhou. At thirteen or fourteen, thrown outside." Huizhou had many mountains and little arable land; boys at thirteen or fourteen had to leave their homes and villages to go into business, returning once every three years, spending little time with their wives. But it was these Huizhou merchants, struggling far from home, who used the silver they earned to build the most beautiful villages in China. The Hongcun Ancient Building Complex in Yi County is hailed as "the village in a Chinese painting" — a cattle-shaped water system winds through the streets and lanes, and the Moon Pond reflects the white walls and black tiles like a mirror. The Xidi Ancient Building Complex, also in Yi County, is known as "the village hidden in the Peach Blossom Spring" — the Hu clan members grew wealthy through business far from home and returned to build splendid mansions. Walking on the bluestone-paved lanes, the Huizhou-style buildings rise tall on both sides — the tears of Huizhou merchants leaving home, the emotions of returning to their homeland, are all carved into the outline of every horse-head wall in Three Words, Two Strikes. The cattle-shaped water system of the Hongcun Ancient Building Complex is a marvel of ancient Chinese village planning: the South Lake at the village entrance is the cow's stomach, the canal winding through the streets is the cow's intestines, and the Moon Pond in the center of the village is the cow's tripe — the entire village's bionic design is exquisitely ingenious. The Moon Pond is a half-moon-shaped pool surrounded by the Wang clan's ancestral hall, Lexu Hall, and several tall mansions. At six in the morning, the surface of the Moon Pond is like a mirror — the white walls, black tiles, and green distant hills are all reflected in the water. Occasionally a white goose parts the surface, the ripples spread slowly — this scene is too beautiful to be real. Standing by the Moon Pond, you think of the Huizhou merchants' wives in Three Words, Two Strikes — their husbands had gone to Yangzhou, Nanjing, Hankou, and would not return for three or five years. Every morning she drew water and washed clothes here, gazing at her reflection in the water, counting the days until his return. Ten li west along the mountain road from Hongcun lies the Xidi Ancient Building Complex. At the entrance of Xidi village stands a three-arch, four-pillar, five-story stone archway — the Hu Wenguang Prefectural Archway, built in the sixth year of Ming Wanli (1578 AD), carved entirely from Yi County bluestone, with stone lions, qilins, and cranes lifelike in the stone. The Hu clan ancestral hall, Jing'ai Hall, is the largest building in the village. The couplet at its entrance reads: "To study well, to do business well — doing well is what matters. Starting a venture is hard, maintaining it is hard — knowing the difficulty makes it easy." The people of Huizhou placed studying and doing business on an equal footing, breaking the traditional hierarchy of "agriculture as fundamental, commerce as marginal." This is precisely the core spirit of Three Words, Two Strikes: not looking up to emperors and generals, not looking down on peddlers and porters, but finding the light of human nature in the smoke and fire of the market. From the Moon Pond in Hongcun to the archway of Xidi, from the hoofbeats of Huizhou merchants departing on distant journeys to the figure of a wife waving farewell at the pier — these are the truest and most moving materials of Chinese literature. If Feng Menglong and Ling Mengchu were to travel through time to today, walking on the bluestone lanes of Hongcun, they would surely find here more stories to move future generations to tears.

stops.title: Stop Six: Shaoxing · The Market Sounds of Yue's Alleys and Lanes
stops.content:
Shaoxing is one of the oldest cities in Jiangnan and a frequently recurring setting in Three Words, Two Strikes. Ming-dynasty Shaoxing was famous for producing private secretaries and scholar-officials. The city is full of deep lanes, old houses, and small buildings along the river. The stories set in the market alleys of Three Words, Two Strikes — the cries of peddlers, the storytelling of raconteurs, the conversations in teahouses — can all be found in the lanes of Shaoxing.

The Former Residence of Lu Xun in Shaoxing is the birthplace of the great master of modern Chinese literature. As a child, Lu Xun loved reading vernacular stories like Three Words, Two Strikes. The lower-class characters he created in The True Story of Ah Q and New Year's Sacrifice share a bloodline with the market crowds of Three Words, Two Strikes. The Hundred-Plant Garden and the Three-Flavor Study in the former residence preserve Lu Xun's childhood memories — the delightful stories he wrote in "From Hundred-Plant Garden to Three-Flavor Study" are like the mischievous pageboys of Three Words, Two Strikes come to life. And Shaoxing's bluestone-paved lanes and small bridges over flowing water are the most vivid geographical footnotes to Three Words, Two Strikes.

The Bazizi Bridge — this Southern Song Jiatai-era stone bridge still serves its function, carrying people across the river in Shaoxing today. Beneath the bridge, black-canopied boats glide slowly past; the boatmen row with their feet and sing Shaoxing folk songs, the same as they did eight hundred years ago. Walk three li along the river from the Lu Xun Former Residence and you reach the Green Vine Studio — the former home of the great Ming-dynasty scholar Xu Wei. Xu Wei's own story is a Three Words, Two Strikes-style legend in itself: a man of extraordinary talent whose life was one of hardship and struggle — mad, impoverished, and down-and-out, yet leaving behind the eternal legacy of the "freehand brushwork" school of painting. If Feng Menglong and Ling Mengchu had met Xu Wei, they would surely have written him into their stories — a man of surpassing talent but a life of misfortune is precisely the kind of character Three Words, Two Strikes most loved and was best at portraying. From the Hundred-Plant Garden to Green Vine Studio, from the Bazizi Bridge to the riverside teahouses — every inch of Shaoxing's soil tells stories like those in Three Words, Two Strikes: ordinary, trivial, yet brimming with deep emotion.
